summary: This document specifies the data formats and code points for the IS-IS extensions used by TRILL. TRILL provides optimal pair-wise forwarding without configuration in multi-hop networks with arbitrary topology, plus multipathing.

plainLanguage.summary: TRILL switches use IS-IS messages to share information about the network. RFC 7176 defines how those messages carry TRILL details, including multicast listeners, VLAN information, and switch capabilities.

subtitle: The IS-IS message formats TRILL switches use to share topology, multicast, and capability information.

tldr.problem: TRILL switches use IS-IS to learn about the network, but need formats for TRILL-specific information such as multicast listeners, VLAN assignments, and supported capabilities.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7176 defines new IS-IS TLVs and sub-TLVs, MTU-probe and MTU-ack PDUs, and rules for using existing IS-IS messages with TRILL.
tldr.outcome: It adds multicast announcements for IPv4 and IPv6, capability announcements, tree affinity, multi-topology support, and fine-grained labels. It obsoletes RFC 6326.

today: RFC 7176 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2014. It obsoletes RFC 6326.

sections.title: TRILL Information in IS-IS
sections.content:
TRILL forwards data frames across multi-hop networks using link-state routing. The switches that run TRILL are called Routing Bridges or TRILL Switches. They use IS-IS to learn the network topology and exchange information.

RFC 7176 specifies formats and code points for the IS-IS extensions that support TRILL. It obsoletes RFC 6326. The update adds group announcements by IPv4 and IPv6 address, capabilities, tree affinity, multi-topology support, and control-plane information for fine-grained labels.
sections.plainLanguage: TRILL switches exchange network information using IS-IS. This RFC specifies the message fields they use to share TRILL-specific information.

sections.title: Multicast Group Address Information
sections.content:
The Group Address TLV is IS-IS type 142 and is carried in Link State PDUs. It contains sub-TLVs that advertise multicast listeners. The six sub-TLV types cover MAC, IPv4, and IPv6 group addresses, each either associated with a VLAN or with a fine-grained label.

A group record identifies a group and may list source addresses. A source count of zero means the listener accepts the group without restricting the source. If the source list does not fit in one sub-TLV, the same group can appear again with additional sources.
sections.plainLanguage: The Group Address TLV tells switches which multicast groups have listeners. Its sub-TLVs distinguish MAC, IPv4, and IPv6 addresses and can identify the VLAN or label.

sections.title: Port and VLAN Information in Hello Messages
sections.content:
TRILL switches exchange IS-IS Hello PDUs with neighboring switches. TRILL carries port information in sub-TLVs of the Multi-Topology-Aware Port Capability TLV. These fields describe the port, VLANs enabled on it, appointed forwarding roles, and the TRILL version and capabilities supported on that port.

The Special VLANs and Flags sub-TLV appears in every TRILL Hello. Other sub-TLVs can list enabled VLANs and appointed forwarders. VLAN ranges treat 0x000 and 0xFFF as invalid values; a range that spans these boundaries is interpreted using the adjacent valid VLAN IDs.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighboring switches announce what each port supports. The announcements include enabled VLANs and which switch forwards traffic for those VLANs.

sections.title: Capabilities and Distribution Trees
sections.content:
Link State PDUs carry information needed across the network. TRILL places sub-TLVs inside the Router Capability TLV or MT-Capability TLV. They can announce a switch's TRILL version, nicknames, distribution-tree counts and roots, VLAN or label interest, shared learning groups, supported RBridge Channel protocols, and tree affinity requests.

The TRILL-VER sub-TLV carries a maximum version and capability flags. If it is absent, receivers assume the base version and no optional capabilities. The same sub-TLV numbers are used in the Router Capability and MT-Capability TLVs.
sections.plainLanguage: Switches also announce information that the wider network needs. These messages describe supported features, distribution trees, and the VLANs or labels a switch handles.

sections.title: MTU Testing and Neighbor Discovery
sections.content:
The MTU sub-TLV, type 28 and length 3, reports the largest successfully tested link MTU or zero if untested. Its failure bit records whether testing failed at the required campus-wide MTU. TRILL uses the TRILL Neighbor TLV, type 145, instead of the standard IS Neighbor TLV in broadcast-link Hello PDUs.

MTU-probe and MTU-ack PDUs can test link size. Their TLV area must be padded to the exact size being tested. TRILL uses a zero area address and includes NLPID 0xC0 in Hello PDUs and LSP number zero. An originating LSP number zero must not exceed 1470 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: Switches report which neighbors they can see and how large a packet the link can carry. Special probe and acknowledgment messages can test the link size.
